summary:
Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act, and both are listed among the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code. Bill C-16 added them; the Senate passed the bill 67-11 in June 2017.

Discrimination complaints in areas of provincial responsibility run through provincial human rights codes. Ontario's code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes a policy setting out the legislation and case law governing complaints under it, so a visitor or resident in Ontario has a documented route to recourse.

Changing the gender marker on official documents is a provincial function. Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the previous surgery requirement and substituted a declaration of the person's identified gender supported by a doctor's letter.
tangentialFactors:
Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, a 1% increase following a 34% rise across 2022-23. Incidents motivated by sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, ending three consecutive years of increases from the 2023 peak of 889. The published national series is not disaggregated by gender identity, so these figures describe the volume of the enforcement stream rather than the level of anti-trans targeting.

Egale Canada's 2012 submission to the Universal Periodic Review recorded that sexual orientation had been read into the Charter since 1995 and that marriage equality dated from 2005, while protections specific to trans people were limited, varied by jurisdiction and lacked any federal prohibition on gender-identity discrimination; the submission set out gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles. That document predates the 2017 federal protections.
localsOnly:
Federal custody rules provide for transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau committed to a review of transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity. Prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. No special-unit, solitary or segregation rule is set out beyond the identity-based placement rule.

Placement and medical care have been litigated: the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh, represented by the lawyer Barbara Findlay, contested placement in a women's institution and access to gender-affirming treatment. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally attentive to trans-prisoner safety and security while some raised concerns about risk to other prisoners. A 2022 CTV report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault.

Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, enacted with the notwithstanding clause, requires schools to obtain parental consent before a student under 16 may use a gender-related preferred name or gender identity; human rights organisations called for its repeal and legal action followed. Alberta's 2024 Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were shielded from legal challenge by Bill 9 (Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025), also using the notwithstanding clause. Ontario's 2012 Accepting Schools Act addresses bullying including that of LGBTQ students, and comparable anti-bullying legislation exists in Quebec, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Yukon.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventoried sources do not set out the federal procedure for changing a gender marker on national identity documents, nor entry, visa or border-screening rules bearing on trans travellers. No trans-specific border or screening practice is documented here.

Two publications are recorded without their findings: Egale Canada's analysis of 2024 police-reported hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI people, and the survey findings of the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan, released as quick statistics.

The national hate-crime series is not disaggregated by gender identity in the material available, so the level of anti-trans hate crime in Canada is unresolved. Prince Edward Island is the only province whose document-change procedure appears in these sources; other provinces' requirements are not sourced.
